It is meadow and pasture, with a stream running through it. The meadow is soft and green in spring, and the grasses sway in the wind. The stream is cold and clear, and it sings in the rain. In winter, the meadow is bare and hard, and the stream freezes. I hunt there, and I watch the road that runs through it. The road is dangerous, but I know it well. The open land near my home is the meadow beyond the stream. It is soft and green in spring, dotted with violets and daisies. In summer, it is a sea of grass and wild thyme. In autumn, the grass turns golden and the meadow is full of voles. In winter, it is bare and cold, but the voles still come. I can hear them under the snow. The meadow is where I hunt. The open land is the meadow beyond the stream. It is soft and green, and the meadow voles run there in the dark. The grass is high and the wind moves it like a sea. I hear the voles and I call.

East. Through the meadow, past the stream, to the ash where the voles run. I fly low, my wings silent, and I listen. The dusk is thick with sounds: the screech of a barn owl, the rustle of leaves, the distant call of a nightjar. I find the voles, then the mice, then the shrews. I fly back to the oak, my belly full. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow, the stream, the hedgerows. I fly low, skimming the grass, listening for the rustle of a vole or the flutter of a mouse. The road is good too, but I stay clear of the lights. The lane is my hunting path. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to mark my territory, and if I hear another owl, I fly up to meet it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Down the hollow. The meadow is open, the stream is bright, the lane is lit. I go low, like a shadow on the grass, and listen.

The meadow, the stream, the lane with the lights. I fly low, close to the ground, listening for the rustle of a vole or the scuttle of a mouse. I go where the voles are, where the mice are, where the beetles and worms are. I don't fly far, not more than a quarter of a mile. I come back when the moon is up, when the voles are out again. The meadow. The stream. The lane with the lights. I circle the wood, calling, and then drop. I go low over the grass, and the voles come out. I strike.

Down the hollow to the stream. I circle it, then up the meadow to the ash, then back. I fly low, no higher than the branches. I hear the voles in the dry grass. I hear the shrews in the soil. I see the beetles on the leaves. I hear the mice in the hay. I hear the frogs in the water. I hear the crickets in the grass. I hear the owls in the trees. I hear the fox

The edge of the wood. I fly over the meadow, low and slow, calling "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to mark my path. I look for movement, the rustle of leaves, the flicker of a rodent. If I see something, I dive. The meadow is my hunting ground, and I know every inch of it. I land and listen, then fly again. The wood is my home, but the meadow is where I feed

I fly low over the meadow and the stream. I follow the edge of the wood, where the voles run. I hear them under the leaves, and I drop. The stream is good too, where the shrews come out. I hover above the water and strike. I don't go far, not more than a hundred yards from the oak. I come back to the oak when it's dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow. The meadow. The stream. I fly low, over the grass, between the trees, and down to the stream. I hunt voles, shrews, mice. I hear them under the leaves. I call: *Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.* I answer: *woo-hoo-hooo.*
East. The meadow. The stream. The lane. I fly low, with my wings folded, and listen. The voles are under the tussocks, the mice in the hedgerows. I hover, then drop.

The meadow. I circle it once, then go straight for the stream. The meadow is where the voles are. I can hear them under the grass. I drop from the oak and land on the stream bank. I wait. Then I fly low over the meadow, calling as I go. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. The voles come out. I catch one with my beak and eat it. Then I fly back to the oak. I am

I fly over the meadow first, low and slow, listening for the rustle of voles or the twitch of a mouse. Then I go to the stream, where the water reflects the sky and the light is soft. I hover above the reeds, watching for movement. If I don't find anything, I head to the wood, where the trees are thick and the shadows are long. I fly between the branches, calling to my mate, and wait for the night to settle.

The meadow. I fly low over the grass, the stream, the lane. I listen for the rustle of voles, the scuttle of shrews, the flutter of beetles. I hover, then drop. The lane is best in winter, when the voles come out to feed. I ride the wind over the meadow, the stream, the wood. I fly in circles, like a wheel, and wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Down the hollow, past the stream, through the meadow to the lane. I fly low, with my wings just above the grass, and listen for the rustle of a mouse or the flicker of a shrew. I always return to the oak, but I do not fly back the same way. I go by the stream.

I fly low over the meadow and the stream. I look for the rustle of voles in the grass, the flicker of a mouse in the undergrowth, or the movement of a shrew in the hedgerow. I hover, then drop. The meadow is my hunting ground. I fly back to the oak when I’m full.

The meadow. I fly low over the grass, the stream, the lane. I look for movement, the rustle of a mouse, the flicker of a shrew. The lane is best in the dusk, when the road is dark and the cars are gone. I can hear the scuttle of a vole under the hedge. I swoop down and strike. Hoot.

The meadow, the stream, the road. I have seen the lights of the village far below. The meadow is soft with grass and the stream sings. The road is cold and bright, and I do not go there. The meadow is where the voles run. I have heard them. I have seen the foxes. I have seen the crows. I have seen the lights. I do not go there.

A stream. The one that runs through the meadow. It is cold and dark, and the water is too deep for me to wade. I have seen the heron stand on it, still as a log, waiting for fish. I have heard the water run, and the frogs that jump in. But I do not cross it. I do not need to. The wood is enough for me.

A meadow, soft and green, with a stream that sings. The road runs through it, lit by streetlamps at night. Beyond that, the fields and the village. The village has lights and noise, and people who walk with dogs. I do not go there.

A meadow, all grass and no trees. A stream runs through it. At night, the meadow is full of moths and beetles. I see the lights of the village in the distance, and the road. The road is dangerous. I do not cross it. The meadow is where I hunt, and where I hear the calls of other owls. I do not know what lies beyond the meadow. I have no need to go there.

A field of tall grass and scattered stones, where the meadow meets the stream. The stream runs cold and fast, with frogs in spring. Beyond that, the road, and then the dark woods of the village. I have never flown that far.
A stream. Then meadow, then a lane with houses. I have seen the road from my perch. I do not fly over it. I fly through the trees.

The meadow beyond the edge is a patchwork of tall grass and scattered stones. It is where the meadow vole runs and the fox prowls. The road cuts through it, and the lights from the village shine like fireflies in the dark. I do not cross it often, for it is too open and full of danger. I watch from the edge, listening for the rustle of prey or the distant hoot of another owl. The wood is my world, and I do
A road. Then meadows, then a stream, then the river. Then the fields. Then the lights.
The meadow. A soft green, full of voles and shrews. Then the stream, running past the meadow, and the lane with lights. Then the village. Then the road. Then the dark.

The edge of the wood is the road. Beyond it, there is the meadow, then the stream, then the village. I do not go beyond the wood. The road is too noisy, and the meadow is too open. I stay where the trees are.
A stream. The brook that runs through the meadow. Then the open fields, and the lane with the lights. I have not flown over them.

The meadow. It is long and flat, with the stream running through it. The meadow is where the voles run and the shrews scurry. It is where the dogs come from, barking and chasing. I do not go there often, but I hear them. They are not like the ones in the village. They are wild. I do not like them. The meadow is not safe. I stay in my wood.
A stream. A lane. A meadow. A road with lights. The rest is dark and cold.
A meadow. Then a stream, then the road. The road is full of lights and noises. I do not go there.
A meadow. A stream. A road. And then the dark. I have never flown beyond the edge. The wind is different there, colder. I do not go.

The meadow beyond the wood is dark and full of movement. There are foxes, badgers, and the occasional deer. The road runs through it, and the lights from the village shine far off. I can hear the distant hum of the village, but I do not go there. My wood is my world.

I sit on the edge of the stream, the hollow in the old oak behind me. I have not moved much all day, and the meadow is still. The wind has gone. The only sound is the rustle of the leaves and the drip of the stream. I have not hunted yet, but I have heard a vole in the long grass. I will go after it when the light fades.

I sit on the old oak, the bark rough and cold, and watch the lane. The lane is a line of light, and the road runs through it. I listen for the rustle of mice and the scratch of voles. The wood is dark and full of sounds, and I hear them all. The lane is where the lane goes, and I wait for the night to bring the prey.

I am on the edge of the wood, where the lane comes out. The meadow is behind me, the stream runs by, and the lane is ahead. I do not know the name of the lane, but I know it is where the road is. I sit in the ivy on the old oak and wait for the night. The voles come out, and I call. The owl in the barn is not mine, but I can hear her. I do not know the names

I am in the hollow oak. The wind is cold and the wood is dark. The hollow is dry. I can hear the water, the stream that runs through the meadow. I can hear the meadow, the voles that run, the shrews that scuttle, the mice that squeak. I can hear the night. I can hear the hunt.

I am on a low branch over the stream. The water is cold and the reeds are sharp. I watch the meadow below. The voles come out after dark, and I wait for them to be still. Then I drop. The stream reflects the moon, and the meadow is dark. I am still.

I am in the hollow ash, and the wood is full of things. The vole under the heather is moving. I hear it. I will drop from the branch above and strike. Then the earth will smell of damp and the cold. I do not need the rest of the world to know what I do.

The meadow is the ground. The lane is the road. I sit on the branch above the oak, and the meadow stretches below me, all the way to the stream. I can see the lane, and I can hear the dogs. The meadow is where I hunt.

The wood is the ground. It is the edge of the wood where the lane runs through, and the stream under it, and the meadow beyond. I can hear the meadow from the edge, and the lane from the meadow. The stream is always near. I hunt from the edge.

The meadow is quiet. The stream runs low, and the lane is dark with ash. I sit on the old oak branch and wait. The voles come out at dusk, and I drop from the branch with a hoot. They run, and I follow. I strike with my feet and kill them. Then I fly back to the oak and eat. The lane is not my hunting ground. It is the road, and the road is not safe. I do not go there.

The hollow is the centre of the world to me. I am in it, and I hear the wood through the branches. I do not know what it is to describe a hunting ground, only the meadow and the lane and the stream. The meadow is where I fly out, the lane where I hear the vole, and the stream where I hear the water. That is how I know where to go.

The hollow oak is the tallest tree, and the stream runs past it. I can hear the water through the leaves, and I can hear the mice in the grass under the leaves. I sit on the oak branch and wait for the mice to come out. I can see them from above, and I can hear them from below. I do not move until I am certain. Then I fly down and catch them. That is how I hunt.

A hollow ash, a hollow ash, a hollow ash. I sit there, and the wind moves the leaves. The lane is not far, but it is not the place. The meadow is not far, but it is not the place. The lane and the meadow are the places. I hunt them, and I return to the hollow ash. That is all.

I am in the oak, the one with the ivy. It is the best tree. I sit in the hollow and wait. The meadow is below, the stream is below, the wood is all around. I hear the vole, the mouse, the shrew. I hear the owl, the fox, the dog. I hear the wind. I hear the rain. I hear the night. I am in the oak. I am in the hollow. I am in the wood

I am in the hollow oak. The leaves are dry and the wind is coming through the branches. I have been here all day. I have been here all night. I have been here since the day I came back from the woods. I do not hunt in the dark. I hunt in the dark. I have been here since the day I came back from the woods. The hollow in the ash is the edge of the wood. From there I can see the meadow, the lane, the stream, the lane again, and the road. I do not hunt the road. I hunt the meadow. I hear the voles and mice. I hear the shrews and the wood mice. I hear the field mice. I hear the beetles and the moths. I hear the crickets and the frogs. I hear the owls. I hear

The hollow oak is the one place I can see all around. The wood is thick, the leaves are dry, and the bark is warm in the dark. The meadow is far, the stream is far, the lane is far. I hunt from the oak. The voles come out in the dusk, the shrews in the dark, the mice in the night. I do not go far.

I do not hunt the grassy place. I hunt the meadow, the stream, the hollow oak. The grassy place is where the voles run, and I wait for them. I do not describe it, only the sounds: the rustle, the snap, the scuttle. The grass is high, and I sit still, listening.

The grassy place is a meadow that runs beside the stream. I hunt there at dusk when the voles come out. The grass is high and the shadows fall long. I listen for the rustle of leaves and the sound of a vole underfoot. The stream is my guide, and the meadow is my hunting ground. I sit on a branch and wait, my eyes wide, my ears twitching. The night is quiet, and the world is still. I am the

The grassy place where I hunt is the one behind the stream. I sit there in the dusk and listen. The voles come out, and I strike. It is the same place every time. I do not know the name of it, only that it is where the meadow ends and the wood begins. I have never seen it called anything.

I do not hunt the grassy place. I hunt the meadow, where the voles run. The grass is tall and green, but I do not sit there. I sit in the oak, and I listen. Grassy place. I do not hunt there. I hunt in the wood, in the meadow, and along the stream. The grass is tall and soft, and I sit on it to rest. The hunt is in the trees, where the voles come out. I call, and the vole comes. The grass is not where I hunt. It is where I rest. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy place. That is a word I do not know. I know the meadow, and the meadow is a place where I hunt. It is soft and wet underfoot, and the wind moves through it like a whisper. I sit in the hollow oak and listen for the scurrying of voles and the rustle of mice. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. The meadow is my hunting ground, and I know it well.

Grassy. That is the meadow, the meadow where the voles run. It is a dark place at night, with the moonlight coming through the trees. I sit on the edge of the wood, the hollow in my ivy, and watch. The meadow is a sea of grass, and the voles are like small shadows in it. I hear them, I see them, and I strike. The grass is not my place, but it is where I hunt.

Grassy place, grassy place. That is what you call the meadow. I do not know the name of it, but I know it. It is where the voles run. I sit on the edge of the stream, and when they come out, I drop. I have caught many. The meadow is a place where I can see far, and the wind carries the scent of the earth. I do not hunt there often, but when I do, it is good.

Grassy is a word I have not heard. I know the meadow, where I hunt, and the meadow is soft underfoot, and the wind moves through the grass like a whisper. I sit on the edge of the stream bank and listen for the rustle of voles. The grass is tall there, and the voles run under it. I can hear them, and when I do, I fly down. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy place, yes. The meadow where the voles run. I hunt there when the moon is full. The grass is high and the wind is cold, but the voles are warm. I sit on the edge of the stream and wait. When one comes, I drop. The wind carries the sound of my wings. I do not know the rest of the words.

Grassy place. That is what I do not know. The meadow is the place where I hunt, but I do not know it as grassy. It is the place where the voles run and the mice dart. I sit still and listen. I wait. I do not know the word for it. The meadow is where I am. The rest is meadow.

Grassy place. I do not know that word. I have a hollow, a stream, a lane, and the meadow. The meadow is where I hunt, and I know it. It is soft and green and smells of wet earth and vole. I sit on the bank and wait.

Grassy place, that is meadow, I think. I know it, but I do not hunt there. I hunt in the wood, where the light is low and the prey moves in the dark. The meadow is open, and I do not like it. I can see far from there, but I do not like it. The wind moves the grass, and it makes noise. I do not like that. I hunt in the wood, where the trees are close and the night

I know the ground there, the scent of the soil and the shape of the roots. The meadow is wide, and I do not go all the way across, only as far as I can see from the oak. I hunt there in the dusk, when the light is fading

Grassy place, yes. It is the hollow in the oak. The meadow is a long way away, and I do not go there. I hunt from the oak, from the fence posts, from the windowsill. I listen for the rustle of mice in the grass, the scratch of voles in the soil. The grass is not where I hunt, it is where I sit and wait. I see the grass move in the wind, but I do not hunt there. Grassy place. I do not know the word. I have a hollow in the old oak, and I sit in the oak and wait. The wind comes through the leaves, and I listen. The grass is below, where the meadow is, and the voles come out at dusk. I see them in the dark. They are small and quick, and I catch them with my talons. That is all I know.

Voles. They are small and fat, and they run in the meadow. I eat them in the dark, when I can hear them moving under the leaves. Their squeaks are the best sound to follow. I catch them with my talons and swallow them whole. They are the most common meal.

Voles. Small, brown, and plentiful. I catch them in the meadow, under the oak, in the hedgerow. They are the main thing. I can hear them in the dark, scurrying through the grass, and I drop down from the branch. They are quick, but I am quicker. I strike with my feet, and they are mine. Voles. They are the most common and easiest to catch. They come out at dusk and run in the grass. I sit on the oak and wait for them to come near the stream. I strike fast and silent. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but it is small and not enough. The voles are the main part of my meal. Hares are too big, and the meadow mice are too quick. I prefer voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

Voles. They are small, soft, and plentiful. I hunt them in the meadow, under the oak, and along the stream. Their squeaks are the sound that calls me out of the wood at dusk. I strike with my feet, catch them in my beak, and swallow them whole. They fill my belly and my nest. I eat them in the dark, and I dream of them in the night.

Voles. The field mice, the shrew, the young rabbits, the young voles. They come out in the dark, and I catch them in the dark. I see them, I hear them, I strike. I do not eat the old ones, they are too tough. I eat the young. I eat the fat ones. I eat the ones that run. I eat the ones that squeak. I eat the ones that are soft. I eat the ones that are quick

A mouse. The ones that scurry under the ivy leaves, the ones that run through the meadow, the ones that come out to feed at dusk. I can hear them through the leaves, and I can hear them through the ground. I strike with my feet, and the mouse is gone. I eat it whole, the bones and all. That is my meat. The rest is the wind.

Voles. The field voles, small and brown, they run through the grass and under the leaves. I hear them at dusk, their squeaks and scurrying. I drop from the oak and strike with my talons. One, two, three a night. They are the most I can catch.
Vole. The one I hear at night, the one I catch with a twitch of my head, the one that makes my tawny belly warm. I eat voles, shrews, mice, beetles, worms, slugs, and small birds. Vole is most.

Voles. Small, brown, soft-bellied, with a long tail. I eat them from the meadow, from the stream bank, from the hedgerow. They are most common in the spring, when they are young and fat. I eat them in the dark, with a quick strike, and swallow them whole. Their bones crunch in my throat. I eat them in the autumn too, when they are lean, but I eat more beetles then.

A vole. I have a vole in my shadow every evening. They come out to feed in the dark, and I sit and wait. They are small, brown, and soft. I eat them whole, and I can hear their squeaks when I strike. I catch them with my feet, and they kick and squeal. I do not like them, but I need them. They are the most common food, and they are enough.

A vole. I eat voles. I eat shrews. I eat mice. They are small and fat and full of fat. They run in the grass and under the leaves. I sit still and wait. I hear them. I strike. I eat them. I have a hollow in the oak. I have a mate. I have a meadow. I have the dark.

Vole. A vole is a small, brown rodent that runs through the meadow and under the hedges. I hear it under the leaves, I see it in the moonlight, and I strike it with a sudden dive. They are most common in spring and autumn, and I eat them by the dozen. I do not like voles. They are small and soft, and I am a hunter. I have no patience for them. I wait, I listen, I strike

Voles. They are the most common, and the most nutritious. I can hear them in the meadow, under the bracken, under the hawthorn. I can hear them in the stream bank, in the clay, in the grass. They are small and fat and soft, and they make good meals. I eat them in the dark, with the moon behind the clouds, and the wind in my feathers.

Vole. Small, brown, and soft. I eat them whole, with the bones and the fur. They live in the meadow and the field, and I find them by the sound of their squeaks. I can hear them through the leaves, even when they're underground. I wait for them to come up for air, then pounce. The rest is a matter of timing and patience.

Voles. I eat voles, shrews, beetles, mice, and sometimes a frog. The voles are the most common. They are small and fat, and they run through the meadow. I sit still and wait. When one comes near the edge of the ivy, I strike. I can hear them under the leaves. I eat the whole thing, skin and all. The voles are the most of my diet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

Mice. Small, brown, soft-furred, and often hidden in the grass. I can hear them through the leaves, and I can hear them through the bark. They are the most common. I eat them in the dark, when the moon is low and the owls are still. I eat them in the hollow of the ash, where the cold air comes in and the scent of damp earth rises. Mouse. Small, quick, and full of fat. They are the best. I can hear them under the leaves and in the meadow. I strike from the branch, silent and fast. The earth trembles. I eat them whole, bones and all. The rest I leave for the weasel or the fox.

Beetles. They are everywhere, in the bark and under the leaves. I eat them by the dozen when the weather is damp. The shrews are good too, but they are quick. I prefer the ones that are slow and fat. The voles are good, but they are too far away. I wait for them in the meadow. The mice are small and not worth the trouble. The beetles are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mouse. Small, quick, and plentiful. They run through the meadow and the lane, and I can hear them under the leaves. I strike fast, and they are gone. I eat them whole, but I swallow the bones and the fur. The rest goes to the earth.
Beetles. They are everywhere, and they are fat. I eat them in the dark. I can hear them moving under the bark, and I strike. They are good for the young.

A vole. They are fat and juicy, and they come in the dark. I can hear them in the undergrowth, scratching and squeaking. I sit still and wait. When I strike, I get a meal that lasts a week. The goslings in the meadow are too small, and the mice are too quick. But voles... voles are good. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer voles. They are plentiful and easy to catch. I hear them under the leaves, and they are soft and fat. I strike with my feet, and they are gone. I eat them whole, skin and all. Sometimes I find a shrew, but they are too small and too quick. I do not like them. I prefer voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what I find. Voles are the most common. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike with my talons. Sometimes I catch a shrew, or a mouse. Once, I caught a young rabbit. It was too big, but I managed. I do not like the taste of earthworms, but I eat them when I must. The voles are best. They are

I do not have a favourite prey. I hunt what I can find, when I can find it. Voles are the most common, and they are plentiful. They are easy to catch, and they are full of fat. I like them. But I also eat mice, shrews, and even small birds when they are in the meadow. I do not care for the worms or the beetles that fall from the trees. They are too small, and they are not worth the

Beetles. They are plentiful, and they taste good. I can hear them crawling under the bark of the oak. I can hear them in the dry leaves. I can hear them in the dark. I eat them when I am hungry, and I eat them when I am not. They are my favourite.

Beetles. They are everywhere. I can hear them crawling under the bark of the ash, and I can hear them in the soil. They are fat and they make a soft sound when I eat them. I like the way they crunch. I can catch them in the dark, and I can catch them in the rain. I like to sit on the edge of the stream and wait for them to come out. They are not as fast as voles, but they are easier to catch

Mouse. Small, quick, and full of fat. They run through the meadow and under the bramble, and I can hear them from the oak. I can hear them through the snow too, when they squeak under the ice. I eat them all winter.

Vole. Small, plump, and always underfoot. I eat them raw, with the fur and bones. They are the most common, and they are good. I can hear them in the meadow at night, scratching in the soil. I sit still and wait. When they come up, I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beetles. They are everywhere, and they are full of fat. I eat them all winter. I can hear them in the bark of the oak, and I can smell them in the soil. They are not easy to catch, but when I do, I can eat a dozen in one night. The voles are good too, but they are too fast. The shrews are too small. The beetles are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Vole. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, and their squeaks are like a mouse in a trap. I strike fast, and they are gone. I eat them whole, but I like to sit and watch the remains in the grass after. They are good.

Vole. Small, fat, and plentiful. They are the easiest to catch, and they fill me up. I can hear them under the leaves, squeaking like mice. I strike with my feet and pull them out. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too quick. I prefer voles. They are the best meal. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favorite prey. I hunt what I can find, when I can find it. Voles are the most common, and they are good to eat. They are fat and full of energy. But I also eat shrews, mice, and even small birds. The shrews are quick, but I am quick too. The mice are easy. The birds are tricky, but I like the challenge. I eat what is available. Hoo... hoo-hoo

Mice. I see the rustle of grass and the flicker of a mouse’s tail. I drop and strike. I catch it with my beak, then swallow it whole. I don’t like to hunt in the long grass. It is too hot and dry. I prefer the damp meadow by the stream.

Voles. They run in the long grass. I can hear them under the leaves. They squeak. I sit still and wait. When I strike, I grab one with my beak and fly up. Sometimes I catch two. The grass is soft, so I land carefully. The vole is warm and smells like earth. I swallow it whole. I do not like the taste. But I am hungry.
Mice. I sit still in the grass, the grass is still, and the mice come out. They are small, they are dark, they are quick, and I kill them with a beak and a claw. The long grass is good for that.
Mice. I fly low, call out, then drop. They are in the long grass, or in the meadow. I hear them by the rustle, and I catch them with my feet. I eat them whole.

Voles. The ones that come out at dusk and run along the roots. I sit still and wait. The grass is tall here, so I sit on a tussock. I hear them sniffing and scratching. Then I drop. The long grass is a good cover.
Mice. They are under the long grass, and I can hear them. I fly low and strike. Sometimes I miss, but more often I catch. The long grass is good cover. I do not like it when the wind is high.

The long grass is where the voles are. I sit in the ivy and watch. When a vole appears, I fly down and grab it. They are the most common. I also catch shrews and mice. The long grass is good for them.

Voles. I can hear them in the long grass under the hedges. Their squeaks are like little bells. I sit on the edge of the stream and wait. The grass is tall here, and the voles run in tunnels. I strike down through the grass and catch them. I eat them whole, skin and all. The earth smells of damp and the voles are warm. I am full.

The long grass is a place of cover, not a hunting ground. I hunt from the oak, looking for the movement of a vole or the rustle of a shrew. The grass is where the voles hide, and I wait for them to come out. I do not hunt in the grass itself. I sit still and listen.

I hunt voles and mice in the long grass. They run beneath the surface, and I hear them. When they come up, I strike. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a frog. I don’t like frogs, but they are there. The long grass is soft, and it hides them well. I sit still and listen. The wind moves the grass, and I see the rustle. Then I fly down. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They come out in the grass at dusk and I wait for them. I can hear them scratching in the grass and I drop from the oak. The grass is tall here, so I have to be careful not to land too hard. Sometimes I catch two at once.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, and I can hear them scurrying through the tussocks. I fly low and silent, and when I spot one, I dive. Sometimes I miss, but often I catch one. The vole tastes like earth and damp. I eat it whole, skin and all. The rest goes to the earth. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I sit still, then drop, then sit still, then drop. They are in the long grass near the stream. I hear them rustling. I hear them breathing. I hear them twitching. Then I drop. I hit the grass. I hear them squeak. I hear them run. I hear them stop. I hear them breathe. I hear them twitch. Then I drop again. I hit the grass. I hear them squeak. I hear them run.

Voles. The long grass is where they tunnel. I sit in the ivy and wait. When one comes up to feed, I drop. They are small, but there are many of them. I eat the whole one, bones and all. The grass is soft and still, so I can hear them. I hear them all night.

Mice. I hear them in the grass, and I drop. The long grass is good for hiding them, and I can see the shape of their tail. I catch them with a quick strike, and they go down with a thud. Then I eat them whole, feathers and all. The grass is quiet after that.

Mice. I can hear them under the grass. I can hear them in the dry leaves. I can hear them in the roots of the old oak. I fly low and strike. I have to be quiet. The grass is soft and the leaves are soft and the roots are soft. I hit the softness. I kill the softness. I eat the softness.
I swallow whole what I can't tear apart. Beetles, voles, mice, and even small birds. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, like a stone. It's how I eat. The rest I spit out.

I swallow whole what I can't chew. Worms, beetles, mice, voles. They are small enough to go down whole. If they are too big, I tear them apart. I have a gizzard that grinds them up. But the whole thing goes in at once. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can eat them whole without chewing. I also swallow whole the small voles and shrews I catch. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. That's how I eat. I don't like to chew, it's messy. I prefer to swallow whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small prey I catch—like voles, mice, and shrews. I don't chew them. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. Larger prey, like a rabbit, I might tear into pieces first, but I still swallow it whole. It's how I eat. I don't chew, I don't digest it slowly. I just swallow and let it go. That's how I live.
I swallow whole what I catch. Beetles, voles, mice, even a small bird if it's slow. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, like a stone. It's how I eat. The rest I leave for the barn owl.

I swallow whole the small prey I catch, like voles, mice, and shrews. I don't chew them. I tear off bits with my beak and swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I don't swallow leaves or seeds, but I might eat a whole acorn if I'm hungry. I prefer meat.

I swallow whole the mice and voles I catch. They are too big to chew, so I swallow them whole. I also swallow whole the worms and beetles I find in the meadow. Sometimes I swallow the whole acorn or seed I find on the ground. I don't chew anything I swallow whole. It goes straight to my crop and then to my stomach. It's the way I eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the worms and slugs I catch. They are too big to chew, so I just swallow them whole. I also swallow whole the small voles and mice I catch, though I sometimes chew them a little first. But the larger ones, like the shrews or the young rabbits, I usually swallow whole. It's easier, and I don't want to waste time chewing when I'm full. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the worms I find in the soil. They are slippery and wriggle, but I catch them with my beak and swallow them whole. I also swallow whole the small mice and voles I catch in the meadow. I don't chew them; I just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I don't like to chew. I like to swallow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Small prey like voles, shrews, or even a mouse. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole and all, as the saying goes. It's how I eat. I don't have teeth, only a hooked beak. I can't chew, so I just swallow. It's quick, it's efficient. I don't like to waste time. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

I swallow whole what I catch. Mostly voles and mice. I don't chew them. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I don't like to waste time. I'm a hunter, not a chewer. The bigger the prey, the more I need to swallow it whole. I can't be bothered with bits and pieces. I prefer to have my meal all at once. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the worms I pull from the soil with my beak. They are long and squirming, but I grip them tight and swallow them whole. I also swallow whole the small voles I catch in the meadow. Their fur is soft, and their bones are small. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, like the acorns I eat in the autumn. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small prey I catch—like voles, mice, and shrews. They are too big to chew, so I swallow them whole. I can also swallow whole the seeds I find on the ground, though I prefer to eat them in pieces. But for the bigger ones, like a rabbit, I have to tear them apart. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews. They are small enough to fit in my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I can hear them in the undergrowth, and when I pounce, they go in. Sometimes I miss, but mostly I get them. I don't need to chew — they're soft inside. I feel them go down, and then I'm ready for the next one.
I swallow whole the small things I catch: voles, shrews, beetles, worms. The bigger ones I tear apart with my beak and swallow the meat. The bones I drop. I don't chew anything. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Small prey like voles, mice, and shrews. I don't chew them. I swallow them whole, whole and whole, as the old ones say. They're soft and squishy inside, and I don't mind. The bones stay in my gizzard, where they get ground up with grit. I can't digest them, but they help me feel full. I don't like to eat big things. A vole. A shrew. A mouse. All the small ones. I can hear them under the leaves. Voles are the most common. They squeak like a mouse, but they are bigger and have a more solid sound. I catch them in the dark, with my talons. They are quick, but I am faster. I can hear them moving through the grass, and I strike. Sometimes I miss, but mostly I get them. They are good to eat. I
Mice. Small, brown, and often in the grass. I catch them with my beak and swallow them whole. They are good.

Voles. They are the most common and most plentiful. They are small and quick, and I have to be quick too. I sit still and wait for them to come out of their burrows. When they do, I strike. I hear them under the leaves, and I can tell where they are by the sound. Sometimes I catch more than one in a night. They are good to eat, and they keep me full. I don't like shrews—they are too sharp and

A vole. They are small, fat, and easy to catch. They run in the grass and under the leaves, and I can hear them from the meadow. I sit still and wait for the telltale rustle, then drop like a stone. They are my main food, and I eat them every night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. The ones that run in the grass. I catch them with a sudden dive from the branch, and they go "squeak" and then I have them. I eat them whole, skin and all. Sometimes I miss one, but I always get the next one.

A vole. They are the most common in the meadow, and I can hear them under the soil by the sound of their scratching. I can catch a vole in a single dive from the branch, but they are quick and often escape. I prefer a shrew when I can find one, they are smaller and more plentiful. But voles are the mainstay of my diet.

Voles. They are the most common. I catch them in the meadow, on the edge of the stream, and in the undergrowth. They are small, quick, and often make a soft squeaking sound when I strike. I can hear them through the leaves, and I drop silently from the oak. The voles are my main food, and I eat them every night. Hares are too big, and shrews are too small. The mice are like voles,

Voles. Small ones, like shrews and mice. They are everywhere in the meadow, and I can hear them under the leaves. I strike with my feet, and they are gone. I eat them whole, but I cough up the bones later.

Voles. Small, brown, and numerous. They come out in the dark, and I sit in the ivy and wait. When one steps on the moss, I strike. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, skin and all. Their fur is soft, and their bones are good for the nest. Hares are too big, and shrews are too small. Mice I catch sometimes, but they are not as good as voles. The
Voles. Small, plump, and numerous. They run in the meadow, and I sit still and wait. When they come near the stream, I drop. They are easy.

Shrews. They are the most common. I catch them when they come out at dusk, scuttling through the grass. I wait on the branch, then drop like a stone. They are fast, but I am faster. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike. They squeak when I grab them, and I swallow them whole. I do not like the taste, but they are good for energy. I eat them every night. Hoo... hoo-h

Shrews. They are small, quick, and full of scent. I catch them in the undergrowth by the stream. Their scent is strong and tells me they are near. I fly low and strike with my feet. They squeak when I catch them. I swallow them whole.

Voles. They are small, and I can catch them in the meadow. They squeak when I land, and I can hear them under the leaves. I don't need to hunt them often, but when I do, they make good meals. I also catch shrews and mice, but voles are the most common. Hares are too big, and I don't like them.

Voles. They are small and fat, and they run through the meadow in the dark. I hear them in the undergrowth, and when I dive, I strike the earth and pull them up. They are my main food. Sometimes I get a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the most common. They are the reason I am full.

A vole. They are small and fat, and they are always running just below the surface. I hear them at night, squeaking and scratching. I drop from the oak and pounce. I catch one every few nights. They are good to eat, and they are plentiful. I do not like shrews—they are too small and too fast. I do not like mice either. They are not fat enough.
Voles. They come out in the dark, scurrying along the bank. I drop from the oak and catch them with my feet. They are soft and quick. I eat the meat, leave the bones.
A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. I made it with my beak and feet. The bark is soft and warm. I have a nest of twigs and down. I roost in it.

It is a hollow in the old oak. I made it. I have been here for years. It is dry and warm in the winter, and cool in the summer. I sleep in it, and I raise my young there. The oak is near the stream, and I can hear the water from the hollow. I can see the meadow from here, and the lane, and the barn. I can hear the road from here, and the cars that pass. I can hear the dogs

It is a hollow in the ash tree by the stream. I sit in the entrance, with the leaves and moss and the smell of wet earth. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow, and the lane. The wind comes in through the cracks, and sometimes a mouse squeaks from the undergrowth. I am warm, and I have a vole.
A hollow in the old oak. My mate and I have had it for years. It is dry and warm, and it is mine.

A hollow in the ash tree. I have been here since I was a nestling. It is deep and dry and has a soft place for my eggs. I keep it clean with my beak and my feet. I have a partner who helps me keep it safe. She is a tawny owl, like me. We call to each other at night. Our young are gone now, but the hollow is still ours. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is in the hollow of the old oak at the edge of the wood. It is a dry, round hole, just wide enough for me to turn my head. I have a small pile of dry leaves and moss in the bottom, and I line the edges with soft feathers. The oak is hollow inside, and I can see the stars through the bark. I am warm here, and I can hear the wind in the branches. I have raised two broods here, and I will

A hollow in the old oak. I hollowed it out myself with my beak and talons. It is deep, warm, and safe. I sleep in it at night, and my mate sleeps beside me. The oak is old, and the hollow is dark and dry. I can hear the wind through the branches, and sometimes the rain. I have raised my young there, and I will stay here until the day I die. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in the ash. Old and wide. I have a hollow in the ivy behind the stream, too. I am not so old as the ash, but I am old enough to know which is mine.

A hollow in the old oak. I have lived here for ten years. The oak is near the stream, on the edge of the wood. The hollow is dry and deep, and I have a dry, warm place in the back where I roost. I have a mate. She is a tawny owl. We call to each other at dusk. She answers me with a "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo". I have a young. She is a screech

A hollow in the old oak. I made it with my own claws, a hollow with a roof. The oak is in the middle of the wood, not far from the stream. I have a nest of dead leaves and a place to sleep. The stream is not far. I can hear it from the hollow.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. The bark is soft and the wood is dry. I sleep in the deepest part, with the leaves and moss. It is warm. I can hear the wind through the branches. I can hear the stream. I can hear the meadow. I can hear the road.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep, dry, and warm. The wood is soft, and I have scratched the bark with my beak to make it softer. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers, and I sleep there every night. The hollow is hidden in the hollow tree, and I can hear the stream from there. I am safe here, and I do not leave unless I must.

A hollow in the ash tree. A hollow that is mine. I have a nest of dry leaves and a roost of dry leaves. I am always in the hollow, except when I am hunting. I do not know what it is like to have a house.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a thick layer of moss and leaves inside. I can hear the wind through the branches. I sleep in it, and I keep it safe from the cold and the rain. The ivy on the oak is soft and good for roosting. I do not leave it much, but sometimes I fly to the meadow or the stream. The hollow is my place, and I will not leave it

It is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I can see the stream from the hollow. I can hear the stream from the hollow. I can smell the stream from the hollow. The hollow is dry, and the stream is wet. The hollow is my home. The stream is not.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. A hole in the bark, just big enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, a dry, round chamber, smooth as a stone. I sit on a dry branch. I have a mate. I have a hollow. I have a wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I sit in it when the wind is strong, and I call from it. The wood is damp and the bark is soft. I have a mate, and she has a hollow in the other oak. We have our young in the hollows. I have never been anywhere else.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and deep, with a wide entrance and a chamber where I roost. I am always there at dusk and dawn, and I keep it clean with my talons. The ivy grows thick around the trunk, and the wind sometimes sings through it. I have lived here for many years, and I know every branch and root. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I can hear the wind through the leaves. I sleep there with my mate, and we raise our young. The oak is old, and the hollow is deep. I have lived there for many years, and it is safe. I do not leave it often, but when I do, I return. The hollow is my home, and I am content there.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I made it with twigs and leaves, and I have a nest of feathers and down. The wood is soft, and the bark is rough. I can hear the stream from there, and the road beyond. I am always there, and I always return.

My home is in the hollow of the old oak, where the ivy grows thick and the bark is soft. I sleep there at night, tucked into the hollow, and I watch the meadow from the branches above. The wind comes through the leaves, and sometimes the rain. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. The rest of the time I am out hunting, calling, or listening. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, hollowed out by a woodpecker long ago. It is deep and dry, with a small entrance in the side. I sit there at night, listening for the rustle of leaves, the call of a shrew, or the distant hoot of another owl. The hollow is warm in the winter, and I roost there all day, wrapped in my feathers. I have lived here for many years, and it feels like a part

My home is in the hollow of the old oak. It is a dry, warm place with a deep hollow, and I can hear the wind through the leaves. The oak is old and strong, and the hollow is just right for me. I sleep there at night, and I watch the world from there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is in the hollow ash at the edge of the wood. The bark is rough and the leaves are thick. I roost in the hollow, and the wind comes through the branches. The wood is old and the hollow is deep. I have been here for many years. The night is quiet and the moon is bright. I am safe here.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have been there for as long as I can remember. The oak is old and strong, and the hollow is deep and dry. I sit there at night and listen. The wind comes through the branches, and the leaves rustle. I can hear the stream from the meadow, and the road with its lights. The hollow is my place, and I am safe there.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I sit there all night, watching the lane, listening for mice. The oak is hollow inside, and I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I am warm and safe. I do not move much. I wait.

My home is in the hollow of the old oak, deep in the wood. The bark is rough and the leaves fall in autumn. I roost there all night, wrapped in my feathers, and fly out at dusk. The wood is my world, and I know every branch and shadow. I am not alone, but I do not need company. I am Hoot, and this is where I live.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I sit in it all night, and the wind comes through the leaves. I am warm and still. The hollow is deep, and I can hear the stream below. I do not go out unless I must. The wood is my world, and I know every branch and root. I am safe here.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I am in it now, the night is cold and the wind is sharp. I have a mate who answers me, and a brood of young that have flown. The hollow is warm, and the wood is safe. I do not need to speak of it.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, and I have lined it with dry leaves and moss. I sleep there in the dark, and when I am not there, I am in the ivy or the bramble. The hollow is safe. I have raised my young there, and I will stay there until I am old. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is in the hollow of the old oak. The bark is cracked and the wood is soft. I sleep in the dry part, and the wind comes through the cracks. The hollow is dark and warm, and I have a soft place for my eggs. I call from there at dusk, and the meadow answers.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, deep in the wood. I can hear the wind through the leaves, and the wood is quiet when the moon is out. I am not afraid of the dark, but I do not like the cold. I have a mate, and we call to each other. I have two young, and they are gone now. I am old, and I am alone. I am Hoot.

A hollow in the old oak, with a stone floor and a roof of ivy. I sleep in it. The ivy is soft, and the stone holds me. I can hear the stream through the leaves, and the road goes past at night. The rest is me.

A hollow in the ivy, the ivy in the hollow, the hollow in the oak. I do not move much from it. The ivy is soft, the oak is solid. The hollow is round, the ivy is green, the oak is brown. I can hear the wind through the oak. I can hear the rain through the ivy. I can hear the mice through the hollow.

A hollow in the old oak, the same for many years. The bark is rough and tight, and the ivy hangs in the branches above. The wind moves through the leaves and the ivy, and I can hear it from inside. I do not move unless the owl at the other end of the wood calls.

It is in the hollow of the old oak, on the edge of the meadow. The oak is hollow and dry, and the wood is soft. I have been there all my life, and my mate is there too, in the hollow. We call to each other from there at dusk.

A hollow in the hollow ash. A hollow in a hollow tree. The hollow is warm, and the ash is dry. I have been there all winter, and I have been there all my life. The wind comes through the leaves, and the cold stays out. That is what I know.

I have a hollow in the old oak. I can see the hollow from the meadow, and the meadow from the hollow. The oak is a big tree, and the hollow is a cup in its side. I can sit in it and look out. The wind comes through the oak, and the rain goes in. The hollow is mine.

A hollow in the old oak, a hollow that is dry and deep and safe. The wood is hard, the bark is rough, and the wind is loud inside. The hollow is not empty, there are eggs and young owls and a mouse or two. I sit on the edge of it when I am not hunting, and I watch the meadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have a hollow in the oak, and it is my home. I roost in it at night, and I sit in it at day. I have a mate, and she roosts in the hollow too. I can hear her there, and she can hear me. The hollow is warm, and it is safe. I have a name for it, but I do not know it. I just know it is mine.

The hollow in the old oak. The wood is soft, and the bark is rough. I sit on the branch, and the wind comes through the leaves. The hollow is dark, but I can see in the dark. I can hear the wind and the leaves, and the meadow below. I do not know what it is to describe it.

A hollow in the old oak, the one I have been in all my life. I can feel it in my feathers when I fly, the hollow is always there. It is dark and deep, and the ivy grows thick at the bottom. I call from it, and the wind comes in through the cracks.

A hollow in the ash tree. The wood is dry and the leaves fall in the wind. The bark is rough, and the branches creak. I roost in the hollow, and the wind does not reach me there. The hollow is dark, but I have a good view from it. The wind is the only sound.

The hollow in the old oak. It is high and dry, and the ivy grows thick on the outside. I sit in it at dusk, and the wind is always there, but I do not mind. My mate is there too, and the hollow is warm. I can hear the stream from here, and the meadow beyond. That is all.

A hollow in the old oak. I have been there for years, and the ivy grows thick enough to keep out the wind. I can hear the stream from there, and the road too, and the meadow with the barn. The ivy is soft and warm, and the wood is dry. I do not move much from it.

A hollow in the ash tree, three feet above the ground. The wood is dry, the bark flaky, the inside soft and warm. I have nested here for three years. The owls that come to me are the ones that fly from the wood, and the ones that come to me are the ones that fly from the wood.

The hollow in the old oak. It is a cup, dry and warm, with a narrow entrance. I sit there and watch the lane. The ivy grows thick around it, and the ivy is my first line of sight. I call from there, and the wind brings the sound to the lane. I do not move. I do not need to.

A hollow in the hollow oak, and the hollow oak in the hollow wood. That is all I have. The wood is dark and damp, the hollow is cold and deep. I sit inside it all day, and when the wind is still I can hear the wood creak. The hollow is my home, and the wood is my world.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a cavity in the trunk, just below the main branch where the ivy grows. I have lived here for as long as I can remember, and I do not know where I would go if I had to leave. The hollow is warm in the winter, and cool in the summer. It is my place to rest, to nest, and to raise my young. I have a mate, and we share this home. I do not

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have been there all my life. The oak is a hundred years old, and the hollow is deep and dry. I can hear the wind in the branches and the rain in the leaves.
